title: Rehras at dusk
hook: the evening prayer, said as the day's work ends

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand Sahib, the song of bliss. Your line was joy, found. Who did you tell your good news to? We've finished the morning. Now the light starts to go. Day one hundred thirty-four.

There's a particular moment at the end of a workday. You shut the laptop, or clock out, or take off your boots at the door. The bag hits the floor. For a second, you're between things: the day's not quite over, the evening hasn't started. Most of us fill that second immediately, with the phone, the news, the next chore. In many Sikh homes, that moment belongs to something else. As the sun goes down, someone lights a lamp, or just sits, and the evening prayer begins. Today, Rehras.
screen: `THE BAG HITS THE FLOOR.` → `BETWEEN DAY AND EVENING.` → `THE EVENING PRAYER BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Rehras Sahib is the Sikh evening bani, said around sunset, as the day's work ends. It's a collection rather than a single hymn: hymns from the Gurus in the Guru Granth Sahib, and then Chaupai, part of Anand Sahib, and a few closing verses. So some of it you've already met this week. It opens with a hymn called So Dar, that door. It's a version of a passage from Japji, and it asks a huge, open question. In paraphrase: what is that door, and what is that home, where you sit and care for all? Then it answers with music. Countless instruments are playing there, countless singers in countless ragas are singing your praise: wind, water and fire sing, the stars and the continents sing. At the end of a long day, when your world has shrunk to your inbox and your sore feet, Rehras opens the window as wide as it goes. Where does the name come from? People explain it more than one way. Some connect it to a word for supplication, a humble petition. Others hear rah, a road, and read it as provisions for the journey. Either way, it fits. It's a pause for the traveler, at the point where the day's road runs out. The instruction the Gurus leave again and again is to hand the day over: whatever you did, whatever was done to you, it rests now in the hukam, the Divine Order. You don't have to carry it into the night. You can put it down.
screen: `AT SUNSET, AS WORK ENDS.` · `SO DAR — WHAT IS THAT DOOR?` · `THE WHOLE WORLD SINGING.` · `PROVISIONS FOR THE ROAD.` · then, large: `PUT THE DAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: Stop for two minutes, as if it were dusk. If it's not evening where you are, pretend. Sit down and let your hands rest in your lap. Think of three things from today, or yesterday: one thing you did, one thing that happened to you, one thing still unfinished. As you breathe out, picture setting each one down on a table beside you. Not solving them. Just putting them down. If you pray, you can hand them over. The bell holds the time.
Rehras. The Sikh evening prayer, said at sunset as work ends, opening with So Dar: what is that door?
Your line: put the day down. This evening, when the light goes, take two minutes before the phone and set the day down, one thing at a time. Day one hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib at sunset, at home or in the gurdwara, as the evening part of Nitnem; it opens with So Dar and includes Chaupai and part of Anand Sahib.

trapdoor: what you thought: an evening prayer.
what it means: a collection of the Gurus' hymns said at sunset, handing the day over as work ends.
what a scholar hears: So Dar appears in the Granth three times, in Japji, in Raag Asa and in Rehras; the name's origin is disputed.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8–12 (So Dar Rehras)

notes: So Dar is found at Ang 6 (Japji 27), Ang 8–9 (So Dar Rehras) and Ang 347 (Raag Asa); the trapdoor says 'three times'. Confirm.
Rehras contents vary between traditions (e.g., Damdami Taksal's longer version); described generally.
Name etymology: supplication (from rahiras/ardas senses) or 'provisions for the road' (rah + ras); presented as differing explanations. Confirm.
'Hand the day over to the hukam' is a summary of a recurring Gurbani theme, not a specific Rehras line. Confirm.
